# 2011–12 Harvard Crimson Men's Basketball Team

The 2011–12 Harvard Crimson men's basketball team had a historically significant season. Here is what I know:

## Overview

- **School:** Harvard University
- **Conference:** Ivy League
- **Head Coach:** Tommy Amaker (in his fifth season at Harvard)
- **Home Arena:** Lavietes Pavilion (Cambridge, Massachusetts)

## Season Highlights

- The team won the **Ivy League championship**, capturing the title outright. This was a landmark achievement as it was Harvard's first NCAA Tournament appearance since **1946** — ending one of the longest droughts in college basketball at the time (66 years).
- They finished with a strong overall record, going **26–5** overall and **12–2** in Ivy League play, making it one of the most successful seasons in program history.

## NCAA Tournament

- Harvard received an automatic bid to the **2012 NCAA Tournament** as the Ivy League champion.
- They were seeded **12th** in their region.
- In the first round, they were defeated by **Vanderbilt**, ending their tournament run.

## Key Players

- **Keith Wright** – A senior forward/center who was one of the team's leading players and an Ivy League Player of the Year candidate. He was the emotional and statistical leader of the team.
- **Laurent Rivard** – A sharpshooter known for his three-point shooting.
- **Brandyn Curry** – The team's point guard who was an important floor general.
- **Kyle Casey** – Another key contributor in the frontcourt.
- **Kenyatta Smith** – Provided depth and interior presence.
- **Wesley Saunders** – A talented underclassman who contributed to the team.

## Significance

- Tommy Amaker's recruiting and coaching had been steadily building Harvard into a competitive program. The 2011–12 season represented a breakthrough, as the Crimson proved they could compete at a high level.
- The season helped establish Harvard as a perennial Ivy League contender; they went on to make the NCAA Tournament in several subsequent seasons as well.
- The long NCAA Tournament drought ending was a major national storyline during March Madness.

## Context

The Ivy League does not hold a conference tournament (at least it did not at that time — it later adopted one starting in 2017), so the regular-season champion received the automatic bid to the NCAA Tournament.

---

This season is widely regarded as a turning point for Harvard basketball and for the perception of Ivy League basketball nationally.
